questions.question: What is the dominant Sunni scholarly position regarding the meaning of the opening letters 'Alif Lam Ra' in verse 1?
options: A. They are abbreviated names of Allah known to all scholars
B. Their precise meaning belongs to Allah alone and was never disclosed to creation
C. They serve as a numerical code embedded in the Quran
D. They indicate the names of the angels who delivered the revelation
questions.explanation: The predominant Sunni position, transmitted through Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, and Ibn Masud, is that the meaning of the muqattaat belongs to Allah alone. This teaching of epistemic humility is itself a spiritual lesson: not all divine knowledge is disclosed to creation, and reciting these letters carries spiritual reward even without knowing their precise meaning.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir argued that the disconnected letters at the start of surahs are part of the Quran's miraculous inimitability because the Arabs, masters of eloquence, could not replicate what was composed from the very same letters they used daily.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir in Tafsir al-Quran al-Azim affirms that the muqattaat constitute part of the Quran's ijaz al-Quran. The Arab audience were masters of eloquence and linguistic artistry, yet they could not compose anything resembling it despite the Quran being built from the same Arabic letters they used every day, making the presence of these isolated letters a direct challenge to their literary tradition.

questions.question: Why did the Meccan disbelievers object to Allah sending a human being as a messenger, and what did Ibn Kathir say was the real reason behind this objection?
options: A. They believed angels were more eloquent than humans and better suited for revelation
B. The objection was not rational but psychological — accepting a human messenger from their own community would require surrendering their pride and social status
C. They had scriptural proof that only angels could carry divine revelation
D. They could not understand the Arabic spoken by the Prophet
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir draws a parallel with earlier nations who rejected their prophets for the same reason: the people of Nuh said 'you are nothing but a man like us.' Al-Tabari records that Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada all agreed the Meccan Arabs used this as a pretext. The objection was a psychological barrier, not a rational one, rooted in the need to preserve social standing.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 3 teaches that intercession with Allah can occur independently of His permission, and believers may call upon intercessors without divine authorization.
questions.explanation: Verse 3 explicitly states 'there is no intercessor except after His permission,' establishing that all intercession is under Allah's exclusive authorization. Ibn Kathir explains this directly refutes the Meccan polytheist belief that idols could intercede independently with Allah, demonstrating that intercession itself is Allah's to grant or withhold.

questions.question: Which theological principle did Imam al-Tabari and mainstream Sunni scholars adopt regarding the phrase 'istawa ala al-arsh' (established Himself above the Throne) in verse 3?
options: A. Complete metaphorical reinterpretation to mean divine mercy spread over creation
B. Tafwid — affirming the attribute as stated without specifying its modality and without likening it to anything in creation
C. Outright denial that the attribute refers to anything real
D. Spatial interpretation placing Allah literally within the physical heavens
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari maintained the tafwid position, affirming the attribute while negating any resemblance to created things and without specifying how it applies. This became the mainstream Sunni position, later codified by Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen summarized the four-part rule: affirm without asking 'how' (takyif), without denying (tatil), without likening to creation (tashbih), and without metaphorical reinterpretation (ta'wil).

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb identified three interlocking symptoms of a spiritual disease diagnosed in verse 7. Which of the following correctly states all three?
options: A. Excessive prayer, neglect of zakah, and avoidance of fasting
B. No hope in the Hereafter, complete satisfaction with worldly life, and heedlessness toward divine signs
C. Disbelief in angels, denial of resurrection, and rejection of the Quran
D. Arrogance toward scholars, abandonment of salah, and hoarding of wealth
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran identifies these three symptoms from verse 7 as a mutually reinforcing syndrome. When hope in the Hereafter is lost, the world expands to fill the entire field of vision; once the world dominates, the signs pointing beyond it become invisible. Wahbah al-Zuhayli adds that 'ittama'annu' (feeling settled in the world) is particularly significant, describing the deepest form of rest misplaced in something transient rather than in the remembrance of Allah.

questions.question: True or false: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi noted that feeling deeply settled and secure in the world contradicts the very nature of the world itself, which is inherently unstable and fleeting.
questions.explanation: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in his Mafatih al-Ghayb observes that 'ittama'annu' (feeling secure and settled) in the world contradicts the basic nature of the world, which is inherently unstable and fleeting. The soul that has found its deepest rest in the temporary has committed a fundamental spiritual mislocation.

questions.question: What does verse 13 identify as the ultimate cause of destruction for the civilizations wiped out before the Prophet's audience?
options: A. Poverty and economic inequality within those communities
B. Military defeat at the hands of neighboring powers
C. Zulm — wrongdoing, most fundamentally shirk and rejection of messengers who came with clear proofs
D. Natural disasters entirely beyond human control
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari explains that the zulm in 'when they wronged' refers most fundamentally to shirk and the rejection of messengers bearing bayyinat (clear proofs). Wahbah al-Zuhayli identifies this as 'sunan al-ijtimaiyya' — Quranic social laws governing civilizations: injustice in the form of rebellion against divine guidance leads to societal collapse. The verse closes with the universal principle 'thus We recompense the criminal people.'

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli argued that the agricultural parable of verse 24 has no relevance to modern times because contemporary farming technology can prevent crop failure.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir explicitly notes that modern agriculture, despite sophisticated technology, continues to demonstrate the truth of the parable: droughts, floods, and blights still reduce crops to nothing. No amount of human planning can guarantee a harvest. Muhammad al-Sha'rawi additionally noted that the verse's mention of destruction coming 'by night or by day' emphasizes that worldly loss comes regardless of human schedules or precautions.

questions.question: The challenge of verse 38 invites disbelievers to produce a surah like the Quran and to 'call upon whomever you can besides Allah.' How did classical Sunni scholars understand the significance of opening the challenge to all possible helpers?
options: A. It showed the Prophet was confident that no jinn would assist the disbelievers
B. It eliminated any excuse that a single individual lacked the capacity, proving even the collective effort of all eloquent Arabs cannot replicate the Quran
C. It was a diplomatic invitation for Arab tribes to cooperate with the Prophet
D. It referred specifically to calling tribal poets and no one else
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari notes that the Arabs, masters of eloquence and poetry, were directly challenged and could not produce anything comparable, which is itself living proof of divine authorship. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi argues that the Quran's linguistic perfection, knowledge of the unseen, fulfilled prophecies, legal sophistication, and literary transcendence together make human authorship untenable. The challenge has remained unmet for over 1,400 years.

questions.question: According to Wahbah al-Zuhayli's commentary on verse 39, what intellectual sin does the Quran diagnose in those who reject its message?
options: A. Excessive philosophical speculation that leads away from revealed tradition
B. Premature rejection — condemning what one has not genuinely studied or comprehended
C. Over-reliance on personal reason at the expense of following established scholars
D. Accepting the Quran selectively while rejecting its legal content
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir argues that premature rejection — rejecting before comprehension — is identified by the Quran itself as a primary intellectual sin. One cannot legitimately reject what one has not genuinely studied. This applies directly to dismissing the Quran based on caricatures or surface-level exposure, which exhibits the same cognitive pattern that verse 39 condemns in the Quraysh.

questions.question: True or false: According to Sunni understanding of verse 62, the awliya Allah are an exclusive hereditary class set apart from ordinary believers by supernatural qualities and special lineage.
questions.explanation: The tafsir makes clear that in Sunni Islam the awliya are any pious believers who fulfill the conditions defined in the next verse — iman and taqwa. Ibn Kathir explains the term derives simply from closeness to Allah through faith and God-consciousness. Ibn Abbas reported that the awliya are those who, when seen, remind you of Allah. The station is open to every Muslim who strives sincerely, regardless of lineage.

questions.question: Imam al-Qurtubi identified three levels of taqwa in his commentary on verse 63. Which option correctly lists them?
options: A. Taqwa of the tongue, taqwa of the heart, and taqwa of the limbs
B. Protection from shirk; fulfilling obligations and avoiding prohibitions; guarding the heart from everything that distracts from Allah
C. Daily prayer, fasting, and zakah as the three pillars of taqwa
D. Fear of punishment, hope for reward, and love of Allah as three equal levels
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi in Al-Jami li-Ahkam al-Quran identifies three levels of taqwa: (1) protecting oneself from shirk, which is the minimum for entering Islam; (2) fulfilling obligations and avoiding prohibitions; and (3) guarding the heart from anything that distracts from Allah. He notes the third level is the level of the siddiqin, and that Ibn Kathir also confirms both iman and taqwa must be present simultaneously — neither alone is sufficient.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 73 records that after Noah's people who rejected him were destroyed, Allah made the surviving believers successors on the earth.
questions.explanation: Verse 73 states that Allah saved Noah and those with him in the ark (al-fulk), then made the believers 'khala'if' (successors/inheritors) after destroying the deniers. The verse closes by asking 'how was the end of those who were warned,' establishing the recurring Quranic pattern that believers inherit the earth when the corrupt are removed — a principle Ibn Kathir connects to the universal sunnatullah operating across history.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb described a three-stage pattern of institutional escalation in Pharaoh's response to Moses, culminating in verse 79. What are those three stages?
options: A. Military force, then economic sanctions, then diplomatic pressure
B. Ridicule and labeling, then political accusation, then mobilization of the most sophisticated state apparatus
C. Imprisonment, then exile, then execution of the prophet
D. Scholarly debate, then popular vote, then military response
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran identifies this escalation: first ridicule and labeling (v. 76), then political accusation (v. 78), and finally mobilization of the most sophisticated state tools — the gathering of all learned magicians under royal commission. Qutb drew parallels to how modern authoritarian systems deploy their media, academic, and propaganda apparatuses against movements that challenge their legitimacy when earlier efforts fail.

questions.question: What made the 'youths' who believed in Moses despite Pharaoh's power particularly noteworthy in verse 83?
options: A. They performed public miracles as proof of their faith
B. They believed and maintained that faith while living under ongoing fear of Pharaoh's persecution
C. They converted through intellectual argument alone after studying scripture
D. They were the wealthiest members of Bani Israel who could afford to defy Pharaoh publicly
questions.explanation: Verse 83 describes these believers as exercising their faith 'ala khawf' — in a state of fear — under Pharaoh's tyranny. Ibn Kathir notes the poignant contrast: Moses faced Pharaoh with complete tranquility while those who followed trembled in fear but believed nonetheless. Their trembling faith is honored by Allah just as much as Moses' serene certainty. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen noted this verse normalizes that small numbers of believers in hostile environments is historically normal, not a sign of failure.

questions.question: True or false: Imam al-Qurtubi derived from verse 84 that Moses' call to tawakkul was a communal obligation addressing his entire people, not merely a private spiritual counsel to individuals.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi, approaching verse 84 from a jurisprudential lens, notes that Moses addressed 'my people' collectively, calling the entire community to a shared posture of reliance on Allah rather than on their own resources or human protectors. Wahbah al-Zuhayli further identifies Moses' approach as 'the prophetic cure for oppression anxiety' — recalibrating his followers' frame of reference from 'how powerful is Pharaoh?' to 'how deeply have you internalized your belief in Allah?'

questions.question: Why did Ibn Kathir and classical Sunni scholars rule that Pharaoh's declaration of faith while drowning was not accepted by Allah?
options: A. Because he did not declare it loudly enough to be heard
B. Because he did not recite the full formula of the shahada correctly
C. Because faith declared at the moment of inescapable punishment is not a free choice and therefore does not constitute valid iman
D. Because Moses had already cursed him and divine curses override repentance
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir cites the hadith from the Musnad of Imam Ahmad in which the Prophet reported Gabriel said to Pharaoh 'Now you believe, when you had been disobedient before?' He confirms the ruling based on Quran 4:18: repentance is not accepted from those who continue in evil until death approaches them. Imam al-Qurtubi uses this verse as the foundation for a lengthy discussion of the conditions of valid tawba, concluding that sincerity, timing, and the absence of compulsion are essential.

questions.question: What made the people of Yunus singular in the Quran's survey of nations that faced divine punishment?
options: A. They were the only nation that received two separate prophets before punishment arrived
B. They were the only entire population in recorded divine history whose sincere collective repentance before punishment descended was accepted, causing Allah to lift the punishment
C. They converted after defeating Pharaoh's armies and were therefore spared
D. They were spared because their city was too large for punishment to be carried out
questions.explanation: Verse 98 presents the people of Yunus as the singular exception: an entire population saw signs of approaching punishment, remembered their prophet's warnings, and turned to Allah collectively and sincerely before punishment arrived. Al-Tabari records they separated mothers from children and cried out together. In response, Allah removed the punishment and granted them more time. Ibn Kathir notes this is the only case in the Quran where an entire town's faith was accepted in a way that benefited them.

questions.question: True or false: Sayyid Qutb described the people of Yunus as 'a beacon of hope' in the Quran's otherwise somber survey of nations that rejected their prophets, proving the door of divine mercy remains open as long as genuine repentance is offered in time.
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran gives this verse one of his most luminous readings, calling the people of Yunus a beacon of hope. He emphasizes their story proves that divine victory does not come to the impatient or to those who compromise under pressure, and that sincere collective turning to Allah before punishment arrives can move the mercy of Allah. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen noted this verse contains the clearest Quranic evidence that accepted tawbah must precede punishment.

questions.question: According to Wahbah al-Zuhayli and Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen, what does verse 99 ('had your Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed') establish about the relationship between divine will and human freedom?
options: A. That human beings have no real freedom since Allah controls all outcomes absolutely
B. That Allah possessed the power to compel universal belief but chose not to, because genuine faith requires freely chosen submission that compulsion would undermine
C. That the Prophet failed in his mission because he did not achieve universal acceptance
D. That Allah's will and human will are equal and independent forces
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir notes that Ashari Sunni theology holds Allah wills the existence of disbelief as part of the created order of freedom and accountability, while simultaneously disliking disbelief and calling all to faith. Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen cited this verse as a proof text against extremism in da'wah: using force to bring people to faith contradicts the divine wisdom embedded in this verse. Ibn Kathir confirms the principle that 'whoever wills let him believe, and whoever wills let him disbelieve.'

questions.question: True or false: In verse 101, Allah commands observing the signs in the heavens and earth as a path to recognizing the Creator, yet adds that signs and warners are of no benefit to those who have resolved not to believe.
questions.explanation: Verse 101 opens with the command 'Say: Observe all that is in the heavens and earth' — a call for deliberate, thoughtful reflection on creation as signs pointing to Allah — but closes with the sobering statement that neither signs nor warners avail a people who have resolved not to believe. Imam al-Qurtubi notes this establishes that the barrier to faith in the hardened heart is not lack of evidence but refusal to receive it, and hidayah (guidance) is ultimately a divine gift sought through sincere openness.
